Belle Epoque Science · Radioactivity Era

Marie Curie

1867 – 1934

Polish-born physicist who, after self-studying in Warsaw's underground Floating University, became the first person ever to win two Nobel Prizes in two distinct sciences: Physics 1903 (with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel) for radioactivity, and Chemistry 1911, alone, for the discovery of polonium and radium.

Born
Warsaw, Russian-ruled Poland
Nov 7, 1867
Died
Passy, Haute-Savoie, France
Jul 4, 1934
Nationality
Polish-French
Known for
Radioactivity, polonium & radium

A Life in Five Eras

Marie Curie lived the European long century. Born in occupied Warsaw and dying in the French Alps the year before her elder daughter won the Curie family's fourth Nobel Prize, her life mapped two enormous arcs: the modern emergence of women in research science, and the discovery of radioactivity itself.

The Sklodowski family in Warsaw, c. 1890: Wladyslaw Sklodowski with his daughters Maria (the future Marie Curie, far left), Bronislawa, and Helena.

Russian Poland and the Underground University

1867 – 1891

Maria Salomea Skłodowska was born on November 7, 1867, in Warsaw, then a province of the Russian Empire. Her father Władysław taught physics and mathematics in a Russian-controlled gymnasium; her mother Bronisława ran a girls' boarding school until tuberculosis forced her to retire when Maria was four. After the failed January Uprising of 1863, tsarist authorities banned Polish-language instruction and forbade women from attending the University of Warsaw at all.

Maria graduated first in her class at the Russian girls' gymnasium at sixteen, then suffered what her sister Bronisława later called a year-long depression. To study at university level she joined Warsaw's clandestine Floating University (Uniwersytet Latajacy), a network of women's classes that met in private apartments and rotated locations to avoid Russian police. To pay for her sister Bronisława's medical studies in Paris, Maria worked for six years as a governess in the rural village of Szczuki, on the agreement that Bronisława would later support her in turn.

"We had a beautiful agreement: when she had her medical degree, she would help me in turn. So I went to the country in 1886 as a governess... I had the principle never to ask anyone for what I could obtain through my own effort." – Marie Curie, autobiographical sketch (1923)
Key Moment October 1891: at twenty-three, Maria boards a fourth-class train carriage from Warsaw to Paris, carrying her own folding stool to sit on. She enrolls at the Sorbonne as "Marie Sklodowska."
Marie and Pierre Curie in their laboratory on rue Lhomond, Paris, c. 1904. The "shed" was an unheated wooden hangar that the German chemist Wilhelm Ostwald later called "a cross between a stable and a potato cellar."

Sorbonne, Pierre, and the First Nobel

1891 – 1903

At the Sorbonne, Marie placed first in her physics licence in 1893 and second in her mathematics licence in 1894. To stretch her scholarship she lived alone in a sixth-floor garret in the Latin Quarter, sometimes fainting from cold and hunger at her desk. In the spring of 1894 she was looking for laboratory space for a study of the magnetic properties of steel; a Polish friend introduced her to a quiet thirty-five-year-old physicist named Pierre Curie. They married on July 26, 1895, in a civil ceremony with no rings; she wore a dark-blue dress she could afterward use in the lab.

Henri Becquerel's 1896 discovery that uranium salts blackened photographic plates gave Marie a doctoral thesis topic. She tested every known element for the same "Becquerel rays" and found the effect intensified by certain uranium ores. Pierre abandoned his own crystallography to join her. In July and December 1898 they announced two new elements - polonium (named for her occupied homeland) and radium - then spent four years processing tons of pitchblende residue in their shed laboratory to isolate a measurable sample. In December 1903 the Royal Swedish Academy awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics to Becquerel and the Curies, the first time a woman had ever received one.

"One never notices what has been done; one can only see what remains to be done." – Marie Curie, letter to her brother Jozef, March 1894
Key Moment December 10, 1903: Marie cannot travel to Stockholm to deliver the Nobel lecture with Pierre; she is ill and pregnant. They go together in 1905 instead. The Nobel citation is the first in any science to name a woman.
Marie Curie, portrait, 1900. The same year she began her solo experimental program on radium emanation.

Solo Career, the Second Nobel, and the Press Scandal

1903 – 1911

On April 19, 1906, Pierre Curie stepped off a curb on rue Dauphine in heavy rain and was struck by a horse-drawn cart. A rear wheel crushed his skull. He was forty-six. The Sorbonne offered Marie his chair in physics. On November 5, 1906, she walked into the same hall where Pierre had lectured, took up his unfinished sentence on radioactive decay, and continued it. She was the first woman appointed to a professorship at the Sorbonne in its 650-year history.

In 1910 she finally isolated pure metallic radium and measured its atomic weight at 226. Yet that year the French Academy of Sciences rejected her candidacy by two votes; the press argued openly that "no woman" belonged among the immortals. In 1911 a Parisian newspaper editor leaked private letters between Marie and Pierre's former student Paul Langevin, who was estranged from his wife. The "Affaire Langevin" exploded into months of headlines. Mobs gathered outside Marie's house in Sceaux. During this scandal the Royal Swedish Academy quietly awarded her a second Nobel Prize - this time in Chemistry, alone, for the discovery of polonium and radium and her isolation of pure radium metal.

"There is no connection between my scientific work and the facts of private life... I cannot accept the idea in principle that the appreciation of the value of scientific work should be influenced by libel and slander concerning private life." – Letter to Svante Arrhenius, December 1911
Key Moment December 11, 1911: ill and shadowed by scandal, Marie travels to Stockholm anyway and delivers her Chemistry Nobel lecture. She is the first person, of any sex, to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
Marie Curie at the wheel of a converted ambulance fitted as a mobile X-ray unit ("Petite Curie"), c. 1914-1918.

Radium Institute, "Petites Curies," and the Great War

1911 – 1918

In July 1914 the Institut du Radium opened on rue Pierre Curie in Paris's Fifth Arrondissement, jointly funded by the Sorbonne and the Pasteur Institute. Marie was its first director. One month later Germany declared war on France and German troops were within forty miles of Paris. With the government evacuating to Bordeaux, Marie left her gram of radium at a bank vault there and turned the unfinished Institute into a workshop for war radiology.

She learned anatomy and X-ray imaging in weeks, learned to drive, and personally equipped twenty automobiles with portable Crookes-tube X-ray sets - the "Petites Curies" of front-line legend. Her seventeen-year-old daughter Irene served as her assistant. Between 1915 and 1918 Marie's mobile units and 200 stationary radiology posts examined an estimated 1.1 million wounded soldiers, locating bullets, shrapnel, and broken bones before surgery. She trained 150 women as radiology technicians, the first generation of female medical radiographers in Europe.

"I am resolved to put all my strength at the service of my adopted country, since I cannot do anything for my unfortunate native country just now." – Marie Curie, letter to Paul Langevin, August 1914
Key Moment November 1, 1914: weeks after the First Battle of the Marne, Marie drives the first "Petite Curie" herself to the front near Creil, ducks the shelling, and sets up a mobile X-ray screening for surgeons within sound of the guns.
Irene and Marie Curie at the Radium Institute, 1925. Irene was already her mother's chief experimental partner; she would share her own Nobel Prize in Chemistry a decade later.

The Radium Institute, the US Tour, and a Death by Discovery

1918 – 1934

After the war Marie returned to the Institut du Radium, where she would direct research for the rest of her life. In May 1920 an American magazine editor named Marie Mattingly Meloney secured a rare interview and learned that the institute owned only one gram of radium worth $100,000; Madame Curie could not afford a second. Meloney launched a national subscription appeal among American women and raised the full amount in twelve months. In May 1921 Marie crossed the Atlantic on the RMS Olympic with Irène and Eve, and on May 20 President Warren G. Harding presented her at the White House with the gram of radium - the gift of one hundred thousand American women, mostly schoolteachers and nurses.

She made a second US tour in 1929 to raise radium for a sister institute in Warsaw. From 1922 she served on the League of Nations Committee on Intellectual Cooperation alongside Henri Bergson and Albert Einstein. She trained the next generation: in 1934 her daughter Irène and son-in-law Frédéric Joliot-Curie produced the first artificial radioactive isotope, work for which they shared the 1935 Chemistry Nobel. Marie did not live to see it. Years of unshielded exposure to radium and X-rays had damaged her bone marrow. She died of aplastic anemia at the Sancellemoz sanatorium in Haute-Savoie on July 4, 1934, at sixty-six. Her laboratory notebooks remain so radioactive they are still stored in lead-lined boxes.

"Nothing in life is to be feared; it is only to be understood. Now is the time to understand more, so that we may fear less." – Marie Curie, address to graduating students of the Radium Institute, 1922
Key Moment July 4, 1934: Marie Curie dies in the Alpine sanatorium at Sancellemoz, the first person known to have died of radiation-induced illness from her own discoveries. In 1995 her remains and Pierre's are transferred to the Pantheon - the first woman interred there on her own scientific merit.

In Her Own Words & Check for Understanding

Marie Curie wrote her two Nobel lectures, a biography of Pierre, and thousands of letters. The four passages below are among the most revealing. Read each one closely; the prompt at the bottom of each card asks the kind of analytical question a teacher would put to a class or you might write about on an essay exam.

Nobel Lecture in Physics, Stockholm (with Pierre Curie)
June 6, 1905 · delayed delivery of the 1903 award · on the discovery of polonium and radium
Our researches upon the new radio-active bodies have given rise to a scientific movement, and have been the starting point of numerous researches concerning new radio-active bodies, and concerning the study of the radiations of the known radio-active bodies. ... It can even be thought that radium could become very dangerous in criminal hands, and here the question can be raised whether mankind benefits from knowing the secrets of Nature, whether it is ready to profit from it, or whether this knowledge will not be harmful for it.
Read closely The Curies refuse to triumph. In a Nobel acceptance lecture they raise the question whether the discovery could be "dangerous in criminal hands." What does it tell you about how the Curies understood their own work that they brought this concern into the Nobel ceremony itself? How does this moment look to you now, decades after Hiroshima and Chernobyl?
Letter to her father, Wladyslaw Sklodowski, from Paris
November 1891 · one month after arriving at the Sorbonne · on solitude and the freedom to study
The garret is very cold; in winter the water freezes in the basin. I cook for myself: a piece of bread, some chocolate, fruit, eggs. I work as hard as I can, sometimes thirteen or fourteen hours in a day. I never feel I have done enough... All my mind is centered on my studies, which, especially at the beginning, are difficult. It was necessary to fill in the gaps of my education, which had not been complete or adequate, and to put myself at the level of the work in the laboratories.
Read closely What two costs and what two gifts does Maria identify in this passage? Why might a young woman who had been denied a university education for years find a freezing Paris garret a kind of paradise? How does her catalog of food and hours tell you about her relationship to her work?
Pierre Curie, photographed by Henri Dujardin in 1906, the year of his death. Pierre and Marie had married in 1895; they shared eleven years of laboratory work and two children. On April 19, 1906, a horse-drawn cart killed him on rue Dauphine.
Diary entry, the week after Pierre's funeral
April 1906 · rue Lhomond, Paris · on the breaking of the partnership
My Pierre, I think of you without end, my head is bursting with it and my reason is troubled. I do not understand that I am to live henceforth without seeing you, without smiling at the sweet companion of my life. ... Everything is over... Yesterday I followed your hearse to the cemetery and I came back to live without you. They want me to take your place at the Sorbonne and to direct your laboratory. I have agreed... and I do not know whether it is good or evil, but it is the only thing I can do.
Read closely Marie writes these lines to Pierre as if he can still receive them. She also reports her decision to take his Sorbonne professorship. Read the two parts of the passage together: the private grief and the public choice. What does the diary's tone tell you about how she experienced becoming the first woman ever appointed to a Sorbonne professorship? Now look at the photograph of Pierre: what does losing the man in this picture mean for her science?
Nobel Lecture in Chemistry, Stockholm (solo)
December 11, 1911 · on the discovery of radium as a new element
Radium, the new chemical element, very analogous to barium by its chemical properties, exists in the pitchblende of Joachimsthal which contains uranium. Its properties make it possible to extract it through the same procedures used for barium. The radioactive properties of pure radium salts are much more intense than those of similarly active uranium salts. The intensity of the radioactivity of radium is so great that all its physical, chemical, and physiological properties are now well known. Radium opens a new world to physicists, chemists, and physicians, and it sets new and difficult problems in cosmic physics.
Read closely Marie Curie speaks here, as the first person ever to win two Nobel Prizes, with deliberate scientific restraint. She does not say radium will transform medicine; she says it "sets new and difficult problems." Then she says it "opens a new world to physicists, chemists, and physicians." What does her order of disciplines tell you about how she imagined her work would be used? Compare this language to the 1903 quote in Card 1: how has her view of what scientific discovery means matured in the eight years between?
